Types of competitions

Competitions in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting range from a friendly club shoot to a world championship. The international rules of both disciplines are written by FITASC, the international federation that governs them. How the sport is organised: FITASC and how international shooting is organised.

A club shoot is a good place to start. Clubs and shooting grounds hold them, often at weekends. There are usually fewer targets than at big events, the pace is calmer, and people are happy to explain what to do. The organiser sets the number of targets, the format and some of the rules, so read the programme.

Next come national events: national championships and cups run by the national federation or by a club it appoints. Their rules are often close to the international ones, and the results may count when the national team is selected.

International FITASC competitions are open to shooters from many countries. They include Grand Prix events and, at the top level, the European and World Championships. An international competition is usually 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25, over several days.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

The 200 targets are shot on eight layouts, one round of 25 on each. At Grand Prix events a “line” is also allowed: a row of 3 shooting stands with 5 traps each.

Compak® Sporting

The 200 targets are shot on eight Compak fields (a Compak is one field with five stations and six traps). The fields are of four kinds: they differ in how many singles and doubles are shot from each station and in what kind of doubles they are. At continental and world championships the host club sets up 48 new machines (six for each field) only for that event, so that everyone shoots in the same conditions.

Big championships rank teams as well as individuals: the scores of a national team’s members are added together. Shooters are also ranked in categories by age and sex. Both are explained in Categories, classes and shoot-offs.

Tip: Many coaches suggest starting with a few club shoots. You get used to the schedule, the squad and the referee without much pressure. How to enter: How to enter a competition.

Key points

  • A club shoot is a good first step; the organiser sets its format.
  • National events are run by the national federation or a club it appoints.
  • Grand Prix events and European and World Championships are international; they are usually 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25.
  • Championships rank individuals, teams and categories.

Did you know?

In Sporting™ the jury may cut the number of targets in an exceptional case. The organiser then refunds the money for the targets you did not shoot, at the price of practice targets.

For the interpreter
  • The level of an event matters to shooters. A FITASC Grand Prix is an international event on the FITASC calendar; national and club events may also be called Grand Prix. Translate the level exactly as the programme states it.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. How many targets does an international FITASC competition usually have?

    1. 100
    2. 200
    3. 150
    Answer

    200

    An international competition is usually 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25.

    Chapter 16 · 200 targets in rounds of 25

  2. Who usually sets the format of a club shoot?

    1. The shooters, on the day
    2. The referee at the first stand
    3. The organiser, in the programme
    Answer

    The organiser, in the programme

    The organiser sets the number of targets and the format of a club shoot, and the programme says what they are.

  3. Why do continental and world Compak® Sporting championships use new machines?

    1. So that conditions are equal for everyone
    2. Because old machines are banned by law
    3. So that the targets fly faster
    Answer

    So that conditions are equal for everyone

    The host club may not use the machines it normally shoots on: 48 new machines are set up for the championship alone.

    Chapter 5 · Championships: 48 new machines
